Colorimetric RT-RPA and quantitative RT-qPCR assays for rapid and field-deployable detection of apple necrotic mosaic virus

Nehala Shaji1 · Rakesh Kumar1 · Damini Diksha1 · Pooja Bhardwaj1 · Jayesh Gehlot1 · Aarzoo Qamar1 · Nitika Gupta1 · Pankhuri Singhal1 · Sajad Un Nabi2 · Virendra Kumar Baranwal1 · Susheel Kumar Sharma1
Received: 3 November 2025 / Accepted: 15 January 2026 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Deutsche Phytomedizinische Gesellschaft 2026
Abstract

Apple necrotic mosaic virus (ApNMV) (species: Ilarvirus ApNMV), the predominant causal agent of apple mosaic disease in Asia, poses a major threat to apple cultivation, leading to significant yield losses. Considering the graft-transmissibility of ApNMV and the lack of resistant cultivars, reliable detection methods are crucial for managing disease spread through planting materials. In this study, we developed a rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable reverse transcription-recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) assay for ApNMV detection. Three primer sets targeting the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and coat protein genes were designed, of which the RdRp-specific primer pair (282 bp) showed high specificity. Crude leaf extracts prepared in NaOH:EDTA (1:1) buffer provided the most suitable template, eliminating the need for RNA purification. The optimized assay performed best at 42 °C for 35 min, detecting ApNMV up to 10–5 dilution in RNA and 10–4 dilution in crude extract template, thereby exhibiting tenfold higher sensitivity than conventional RT- PCR. No cross-reactivity was observed with other common apple viruses (ASPV, ASGV, ACLSV, ApMV). ApNMV was detected by RT-RPA in 75% (55 of 73) of field samples compared to 71% (52 of 73) by RT-PCR. For on-site application, the assay was coupled with the hydroxy naphthol blue (HNB) dye, producing distinct colour changes for positive and negative reactions, fully concordant with gel electrophoresis. In parallel, a SYBR Green-based RT-qPCR assay targeting RdRp gene was developed for absolute quantification, yielding a robust standard curve (R2 = 0.99, efficiency = 98.6%) and detecting viral loads ranging from 12.9 to 86.9 copies in field samples. Collectively, RT-RPA offers a rapid, simple, and field-adaptable diagnostic tool, while RT-qPCR enables precise quantification, together supporting enhanced surveillance and management of ApNMV in apple production systems.
Keywords Apple necrotic mosaic virus · RT-RPA · Colorimetric assay · RT-qPCR · Field-deployable detection · Crude extract · Molecular diagnostics · Apple mosaic disease
Introduction

The domesticated apple (Malus × domestica Borkh) of the family Rosaceae is the most widely cultivated temperate fruit crop worldwide. Apples are rich in vitamins, miner- als, and phytochemicals, that contribute to their nutritional

values and antioxidant potential (Boyer and Liu 2004). Regarded as the king of temperate fruits, apples are highly praised for their delicious flavour and strong global demand, which makes them a potential export commodity (Man- zoor et al. 2025). Temperate fruit belts worldwide, includ- ing India, rely on apple cultivation as a primary source of income and livelihood. India holds a remarkable position, ranking as one of the world's top five apple-producing coun- tries, with an output of 2.87 million metric tons, contributing 2.68% to global production (FAOSTAT 2026). In India, the northwestern Himalayan regions, specifically Jammu and Kashmir, and Himachal Pradesh contribute over 95% of the country’s apple production.
Apple productivity has been hampered by several dis- eases caused by viruses and virus-like pathogens. Apple

trees are known to be infected by more than 20 viruses, among them apple mosaic disease (AMD) is the economi- cally most significant viral disease of apple with widespread incidence leading to 30–40% yield losses (Chai et al. 2017; Nabi et al. 2020; Khan et al. 2024a). The AMD is charac- terized by pale yellow to cream coloured irregular spots or bands along veins, mosaic, and necrosis on the leaves of infected apple trees. The disease causes damage to meso- phyll cell structure and significantly reduces the leaf chloro- phyll content, which diminishes the net photosynthetic rate and ultimately reduces yield (Liu et al. 2023). ApNMV is a newly identified virus that is notable for its prevalence and widespread distribution in mosaic-infected apple orchards across Asia (Noda et al. 2017; Cho et al. 2017; Xing et al. 2018; Shi et al. 2020; Nabi et al. 2020). ApNMV, a posi- tive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the genus Ilarvi- rus (family Bromoviridae) is characterized by a tripartite genome and quasispherical particles of diameter 25–29 nm (Fauquet and Fargette 2005). ApNMV is transmissible by grafting, but no vectors or alternative transmission modes
have been reported to date (Manzoor et al. 2023).

The rising incidence of ApNMV in mosaic-infected Indian apple orchards poses a major threat to the orchard's health. As apple is commercially propagated through cut- tings and grafting, and effective resistance against ApNMV is not yet available, the production and use of virus-free planting materials are essential for sustainable manage- ment of AMD (Hu et al. 2019; Manzoor et al. 2023). Rapid and sensitive detection of ApNMV in the planting materi- als is crucial to prevent the entry and spread of virus into new orchards. Several molecular techniques (RT-PCR, RT-qPCR) and high-throughput sequencing (HTS)-based approaches have been employed to detect the viruses asso- ciated with AMD (Noda et al. 2017; Shi et al. 2020; Nabi et al. 2022, 2023; Khan et al. 2024b). However, each method has its own limitations, viz., the need for purified nucleic acid as template, reliance on costly thermal cyclers with strict thermal cycling conditions, requirement for bioinfor- matics expertise, and time-consuming sample processing, which hinder their routine applicability (Liu et al. 2021).

Recently, diverse isothermal nucleic acid amplification- based detection methods based on different enzymatic processes have been developed, among which recombi- nase polymerase amplification (RPA) stands out as a rapid, simple, and efficient tool for detecting plant viruses. The isothermal amplification is facilitated by the combination of proteins and enzymes, viz., the single-stranded bind- ing proteins (SSB), recombinase, strand-displacing poly- merase, and a pair of target-specific primers (Piepenburg et al. 2006). The reverse transcription RPA (RT-RPA) assay enables amplification of target RNA regions at 37–42 °C within minutes, with efficiency influenced by template

concentration and amplicon size (Diksha et al. 2024). The reaction does not require a thermal cycler and can be per- formed using simple equipment such as heating blocks, dry-bath, or water-bath. RPA detection has been success- fully employed for the detection of several DNA and RNA viruses infecting horticultural crops viz., bean golden yel- low mosaic virus (Londoño et al. 2016), banana bunchy top virus (Kapoor et al. 2017), apple stem grooving virus (Kim et al. 2018), citrus concave gum-associated virus (Liu et al. 2021), citrus tristeza virus (Sharma et al. 2023), grapevine virus B (Thapa et al. 2024), citrus yellow vein clearing virus (Gupta et al. 2024) etc. In the present study, we developed an RT-RPA assay for rapid and robust detection of ApNMV with crude plant extract as template coupled with colorimet- ric detection via naked eye by the addition of HNB dye. This approach eliminates the need for gel electrophore- sis and makes this assay field deployable. The developed colorimetric RT-RPA assay was comparatively evaluated through RT-PCR as well as RT-qPCR.
Materials and methods
Plant materials and sample processing

Apple leaf samples were collected from various apple orchards in the major apple-growing regions of Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh. Leaves exhibiting virus-like symptoms, including mosaic patterns, mosaic with necrosis, vein banding producing a reticulated appearance, and curl- ing as well as asymptomatic samples were collected from commercially cultivated varieties (Fig. 1A). The presence of ApNMV infection was initially confirmed by RT-PCR using the specific primer pair, ApNMV_RNA1_F 5′–3′: C A G G A A G G C C G A G T A C G T G A and ApNMV_RNA1_R 5′–3′: A G T C T T C C A C A C C C T C A A C G, targeting the conserved region of partial REP gene (470 bp) of ApNMV (Khan et al. 2024a). A plant sample from the cultivar Red Delicious, which tested positive, and a sample from the cultivar Ambri, which tested negative for ApNMV infection, were used as positive and healthy controls, respectively, for the standard- ization of the RT-RPA assay and subsequent experiments conducted during the course of study. For further investiga- tion, the collected samples were stored at 4 °C and −80 °C, depending on the purpose of study.
RNA isolation

Total RNA was isolated from infected and healthy apple leaf tissues (100 mg/sample) using the Spectrum™ Plant Total RNA kit (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA) with a modified lysis buffer containing 2% polyvinylpyrrolidone following

Crude plant extract preparation

To detect ApNMV using crude plant extract as template, six distinct lysis buffers were evaluated for template prepara- tion, namely: 0.5 M NaOH (Kapoor et al. 2017), Spectrum™ Plant Total RNA kit lysis buffer (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA), 0.1 M Phosphate buffer (pH 7.4), NaOH:EDTA buf- fer in two ratios (1:1 and 1:2), corresponding to 50 mM NaOH and 2.5 mM EDTA (pH 8.0) (Sharma et al. 2023), and MacKenzie buffer (MacKenzie et al. 1997). To homogenise, 100 mg of fresh apple leaf tissue was ground in a sterile mortar and pestle with 1 mL of each lysis buffer (1:10 w/v). The extract was transferred to a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube and centrifuged at 10,000 g for 5 min. The superna- tant was collected without disturbing the particulate matter settled at the bottom of the tube and transferred to a sterile

Primer designing for RT-RPA assay

For RT-RPA, three sets of primers were designed target- ing the CP and RdRp genes of ApNMV, based on mul- tiple sequence alignments of ApNMV isolates retrieved from GenBank database (Table S1). Primers were manu- ally designed following the manufacturer’s guidelines (www.twistdx.co.uk) and further evaluated in silico using BLASTn for their specificity ( h t t p : / / w w w . n c b i . n l m . n i h . g o v t / b l a s t). Designed primers were synthesized by Barcode Bio- sciences (Bengaluru, Karnataka, India).
Primer validation using standard RT-PCR assay

The manually designed primers for RT-RPA assay were initially validated by standard RT-PCR to identify the specific primer set for ApNMV detection. For this pur- pose, cDNA synthesized from ~200 to 500 ng of isolated RNA of ApNMV-positive and healthy samples employ- ing FIRE Script® RT cDNA synthesis kit (Solis BioDyne
ay Springer
Page 4 of 13

OÜ, Teaduspargi, Estonia) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines was used as template. Subsequently, RT-PCR was carried out in a reaction cocktail of 25 µL consisting of 12.5 µL of 2X DreamTaq PCR Master Mix (Thermo- Fisher Scientific, USA), 8.5 µL nuclease-free water, 2 µL cDNA template (~100 ng/µL), and 1 µL each of forward and reverse primers (10 µM). The thermal cycling condi- tions comprised an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 4 min followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 94 °C for 35 s, annealing at 60 °C for 35 s, and extension at 72 °C for 35 s, followed by a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. The result- ing RT-PCR products were electrophoresed in 2% agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide, and visualized using a gel documentation system Gel Doc XR+ (Bio-Rad Labora- tories, California, USA) under UV light.
Reverse transcription-recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) assay

The primer pairs that gave targeted amplification in RT-PCR were further tested in RT-RPA assay to select the best primer set. RT-RPA assay was performed using TwistAmp® Basic RPA kit (TwistDx, Cambridge, UK) according to the manu- facturer’s guidelines. The reaction mixture consisted of 2.4 µL of forward primer and reverse primer each (10 µM), 29.5 µL of rehydration buffer, and 10.7 µL of sterile distilled water to make a final volume of 45 µL. The freeze-dried pel- lets containing RT-RPA reagents were added to this mixture, followed by thorough mixing. The reaction mixture was further halved into two reaction tubes (22.5 µL), followed by the addition of 1 µL of template [either 100 ng RNA or 100 mg/mL of crude plant extract lysed in NaOH: EDTA (1:1) buffer]. To amplify the RNA virus ApNMV, reverse transcriptase (1 µL) was also added. Finally, the reac- tion was initiated by adding 1.5 µL of magnesium acetate (280 mM) and incubated at 42 °C for 35 min in a heating block for amplification. Each RT-RPA assay was carried out using three biological replicates in the present study. After heat inactivation of reactions at 65 °C for 10 min, the RT- RPA products were combined with 6X DNA loading dye and visualized on a 2% agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide under UV illumination. Further, the RT-RPA ampli- cons were gel-purified and cloned into the pGEM-T Easy vector (Promega, Madison, USA) according to the manufac- turer’s protocol. The positive clones were sequenced in both forward and reverse directions using the universal primers T7 and SP6, respectively, and the sequences were analysed using the BLASTn tool of NCBI, GenBank nucleotide data- base (http:// www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ blast) for confirmation.

Comparison of crude plant extract prepared in different lysis buffers as template in RT-RPA assay

The confirmed ApNMV positive sample was lysed in 6 dis- tinct lysis buffers (as mentioned above), and 2 µL of the resulting crude plant extract was used as template in RT- RPA assay. Out of all the crude sap extracted in respective lysis buffers, the one that gave specific amplification was selected as best crude plant extract template for further validations. The crude leaf extract from plant sample found RT-PCR negative for ApNMV prepared in respective lysis buffers was included as healthy controls.
Comparison of different incubation temperatures and time periods for ApNMV detection using RT-RPA assay

The RT-RPA assay was performed using both RNA and crude plant extract prepared in NaOH: EDTA (1:1) from ApNMV positive sample as templates across different incu- bation temperatures, i.e., 25, 28, 30, 35, 37, and 42 °C for 35 min to determine the best incubation temperature to per- form RT-RPA for ApNMV detection. Similarly, optimum incubation time periods were also ascertained by perform- ing RT-RPA reactions for different time periods, i.e., 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40 min, at an isothermal tempera- ture of 42 °C. Both RNA and crude plant extract in NaOH: EDTA (1:1) from ApNMV negative sample were used as healthy controls to check non-specific amplification.
Comparison of analytical sensitivity and specificity of RT-RPA and RT-PCR

Sensitivity of the RT-RPA assay was compared with RT- PCR using ten-fold serial dilutions (100 to 10−8) of purified RNA (initial concentration 100 ng/µL) and crude leaf extract (100 mg/mL tissue homogenate in NaOH: EDTA, 1:1) from ApNMV positive samples as templates. In these assays, the crude leaf extract and purified RNA from ApNMV nega- tive sample were used as healthy controls. The experiments on analytical sensitivity were repeated thrice. All assays were performed under standardized conditions as described above. To evaluate the specificity of the developed RT-RPA assay, cross-reactivity of primer pair ApNMV_RPA_F1/R1 was tested against the most common apple-infecting viruses, i.e., apple stem pitting virus (ASPV), apple stem grooving virus (ASGV), apple chlorotic leaf spot virus (ACLSV)), and apple mosaic virus (ApMV). The specificity analysis of RT-RPA assay was performed using crude leaf extract from samples positive for respective viruses as templates, includ- ing a healthy control.

Validation of RT-RPA assay for robust detection of ApNMV using field samples

Standardized RT-RPA assay was validated for its robust detection of ApNMV infection in 73 suspected apple leaf samples (symptomatic and asymptomatic) collected from various apple orchards of Jammu and Kashmir and Him- achal Pradesh, consisting of major apple varieties cultivated in India. RT-RPA assays were carried out using both RNA and crude extracts prepared in NaOH: EDTA (1:1) as tem- plates following the optimum reaction conditions. RT-PCR was performed in parallel for all the samples using cDNA prepared from the total RNA of leaf samples as templates employing the primer pair ApNMV_RNA1_F/R, as men- tioned above. The amplicons were separated in 2% agarose gel electrophoresis and visualized in Gel Doc XR+ (Bio- Rad Laboratories Inc., USA).
Colorimetric end-point detection of RT-RPA assay

To enable on-site detection without electrophoresis, RT- RPA was further optimized with HNB (Sisco Research Lab- oratories Pvt. Ltd., India) dye-based colorimetric readout, following protocol by Kumar et al. (2025a, b). To a 25 µL reaction volume, 1 µL of 3 mM HNB was added before amplification and mixed thoroughly by pipetting. The reac- tion was incubated at 42 °C for 35 min, followed by heat inactivation at 65 °C for 10 min.
Development and optimization of a SYBR Green-based reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) assay

The RdRp gene fragment of about 282 bp of ApNMV was amplified using gene-specific primers, ApNMV_RPA_F1/ R1, and cloned into the pGEM-T Easy vector (3015 bp) (Promega, USA). Recombinant plasmid DNA was purified using the QIAprep Spin Miniprep Kit (Qiagen, Germany) and quantified with a NanoDrop™ One Spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Wilmington, USA). As suggested by Li et al 2009, the copy number of plasmid DNA was calculated using the following formula: Copies/µL = [Amount (ng) × 6 .022 × 1023/Length of amplicon (bp) × 1 × 109 × 650]. Based on this calculation, ten-fold serial dilutions of plasmid DNA ranging from 100 to 0.00001 ng/µL were prepared and used for constructing a standard curve. Each dilution was tested in triplicate using SYBR Green RT-qPCR, along with non-template control as negative control (N). The mean cycle threshold (Ct) values were plotted against the logarithm (base 10) of calculated copy numbers of plasmids to construct the standard curve. These dilutions served as
Page 5 of 13 34
quantitative standards for absolute quantification of viral load in test samples.

The generated standard curve was subsequently used to quantify the viral load in symptomatic leaf samples col- lected from different apple plants. The relationship between the Ct values and the log₁₀ of the copy number was defined by the standard curve equation: y = mx + b; Ct = m × log10 (copy number) + b, where y is the Ct value, x is the log10 (copy number), m is the slope and b is the y-intercept of the standard curve. To estimate the viral copy number in each sample, the equation was rearranged as: log10 (copy number) = (Ct − b)/m, followed by calculation of the abso- lute copy number using: copy number = 10[(Ct−b)/m] (Li et al. 2009; Kumar et al. 2026). For RT-qPCR efficiency and analytical sensitivity, the linear regression equation and cor- relation coefficient (R2) were determined. Amplification efficiency (E) of the assay was calculated using the equa- tion: E = 10 (−1/slope) and the percent efficiency was calcu- lated as: % E = (E − 1) × 100.

The developed RT-qPCR assay was validated using representative field samples that were previously tested positive by RT-RPA and RT-PCR. A total of 12 apple leaf samples, along with positive and negative controls, were included in the analysis. For comparative evaluation, RT- RPA and RT-PCR assays were also performed on the same samples using the identical primer set under the standard- ized conditions described above. RT-qPCR assay was per- formed using the Maxima SYBR Green/ROX qPCR Master Mix (2X) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) using the primer set ApNMV_RPA_F1/R1. The 15 µL reaction mixture con- sisted of 1 µL of template (serially diluted plasmid/ cDNA of field samples), 0.5 µL each of forward and reverse prim- ers (10 µM), 8.0 µL Maxima SYBR Green/ROX qPCR master mix (2X) and 5 µL of nucleus-free water. The ther- mal cycling profile included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 20 s, annealing at 60 °C for 15 s, and extension at 72 °C for 15 s followed by a melting stage.
Results
Primer specificity

The apple leaf samples that tested positive in standard RT- PCR amplifying the partial RdRp gene (Khan et al. 2024a, b) were used in all RT-RPA assays conducted in this study. Validation of RT-RPA primers through RT-PCR revealed that the primer pairs ApNMV_RPA_F1/R1 (~282 bp) and ApNMV_CP_F2/R2 (~167 bp) showed targeted amplifica- tion, whereas in RT-RPA, the primer pair ApNMV_RPA_ F1/R1 yielded specific amplification of an approximately

Page 6 of 13

282 bp fragment. No amplification was observed in healthy controls, compared to the other primer pair ApNMV_CP_ F2/R2 which showed non-specific amplification (Fig. 1B). The specific amplicons obtained from positive samples were cloned and sequenced. The sequencing results were further analysed using BLASTn, which revealed >99.23% iden- tity with the corresponding ApNMV-RdRp gene sequence (Accession No. OR889827.1), thereby confirming the viral origin. The results thus confirmed the functionality of the ApNMV_RPA_F1/R1 primers and indicated that they were subsequently selected for all the RT-RPA and RT-qPCR experiments used in this study.
Standardization of different lysis solutions for simplified template preparation for RT-RPA assay

Crude leaf extracts were prepared from both ApNMV-posi- tive and healthy (RT–PCR negative) samples using six dif- ferent lysis buffers, enabling their direct use as templates in RT-RPA assays. Among all the lysis buffers tested, crude leaf extract prepared in a NaOH: EDTA (1:1) buffer con- sistently yielded brighter and clearer, target-specific ampli- fication of ~282 bp on agarose gel, whereas other buffers showed weak or no amplification. Therefore, NaOH: EDTA (1:1) was considered the optimal lysis buffer for the prepa- ration of crude extracts for RT-RPA and was used in the sub- sequent experiments (Fig. 1C).
Optimization of the incubation temperature and time period for RT-RPA assay-based detection of ApNMV

The crude leaf extract prepared in NaOH: EDTA (1:1) buf- fer and purified RNA from ApNMV positive sample and healthy (RT-PCR negative) sample were used as templates to determine the optimal incubation temperature and time period for RT-RPA assay. The RT-RPA assay employing ApNMV_RPA_F1/R1 primer pair was performed across different incubation temperature ranges from 25 to 42 °C for a constant period of 35 min. Even though amplification was observed between 37 and 42 °C, the most significant product (brighter and sharper) was obtained at 42 °C after 35 min, where a specific amplification of about 282 bp was observed on a 2% agarose gel. Similarly, RT-RPA was also performed to ascertain the optimum incubation time, by incubating the reactions for different time periods of 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 35 min while keeping an isothermal tem- perature of 42 °C. The results showed amplification starting from as early as 15 min with brighter bands at 35 min, as visualized on 2% agarose gel. Hence, the optimized RT- RPA conditions were established at 42 °C for 35 min for the detection of ApNMV.

Comparative analytical sensitivity and specificity of the developed RT-RPA assay

The analytical sensitivity of the developed RT-RPA assay was compared with RT-PCR using templates from ApNMV positive samples, specifically RNA (initial concentration: ~100 ng/µL) and crude extract prepared in NaOH: EDTA 1:1 (100 mg leaf tissue lysed in 1 mL of lysis buffer), using ten-fold serial dilutions ranging from 100 to 10–8. The results showed that ApNMV was detected by RT-RPA up to 10–4 dilution while no amplicon was obtained by RT-PCR using the same crude plant extract template (Fig. 2a, b). With purified RNA as template, amplification was observed up to 10–5 (1 pg/µL) and 10–3 (100 pg/µL) dilutions in RT- RPA and RT-PCR, respectively (Fig. 2c, d). These findings indicated that RT-RPA shows higher sensitivity and efficacy compared with conventional RT-PCR for the detection of ApNMV from apple samples.

The specificity test of the developed RT-RPA assay showed that specific amplification of ApNMV was achieved by RT-RPA in apple samples infected with ApNMV, and no amplifications were observed in samples infected with ASPV, ASGV, ACLSV, and ApMV. Even ApNMV positive samples were having mixed infection of these other viruses, developed RT-RPA has specifically amplified ~282 bp par- tial RdRp gene of ApNMV. The results were further con- firmed through Sanger sequencing and NCBI BLASTn analysis. This shows the developed assay’s specificity and reliability for the detection of ApNMV.
Validation of crude extract-based RT-RPA assay combined with colorimetric end-point detection of ApNMV using field samples

Field validation of the crude sap-based RT-RPA assay was carried out using different symptomatic and asymptomatic leaf samples from different cultivars of apple collected from Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh. Detec- tion of ApNMV from the collected samples was performed by using RT-RPA assay as well as conventional RT-PCR in parallel. The RT-RPA assay gave positive reaction for 55 out of 73 samples collected (data not shown), showing an incidence of 75.3%, compared to 52 samples found posi- tive in RT-PCR (incidence 71.2%). Thus, the results showed that the developed RT-RPA assay is more sensitive and efficient than RT-PCR (Table 1). Test results indicated the widespread distribution of ApNMV in different cultivars of apple across major apple orchards in India. Moreover, RT- RPA was optimized for colorimetric endpoint detection with HNB dye to enhance on-site accessibility. Amplification was consistently observed across the full range of dilutions, with Ct values from 3.254 to 27.16 (Table S2, Fig. 4a). Melt curve analysis exhibited a nearly single distinct peak for each dilution, thereby confirming the specificity of the assay and ruling out non-specific amplifi- cation or primer-dimer formation (Fig. 4a). The Ct values obtained at each dilution exhibited a linear relationship with the logarithm of plasmid copy number (Fig. 4b). The regression equation derived from the standard curve was: Ct = −3.354 × log10(copy number) + 30.155, with a coeffi- cient of determination (R2) value of 0.9988, indicating high linearity and reproducibility of the assay. The slope value of −3.354 corresponds to a PCR efficiency of 98.64%, which was calculated as: E = (10–1/slope − 1) × 100. An efficiency in the range of 90–110% is generally considered accept- able, confirming the reliability of the assay. The detectable range of dilution is from 2.81 × 1010 to 2.81 × 103 copies/µL (Fig. 4c). This standard curve was subsequently employed for quantification of unknown test samples, using the for- mula: Copy Number = 10(Ct−30.155)/−3.354.

Quantitative detection of ApNMV by two step RT-qPCR

The two step RT-qPCR successfully detected ApNMV in all 12 symptomatic apple samples tested. Ct values ranged from 23.65 (S8) to 26.43 (S2), corresponding to viral copy numbers of approximately 86.90 copies (S8) to 12.89 cop- ies (S2). Samples S3, S4, S7 and S9 showed relatively high viral titers (1.59–1.80 log10 copies), while S1, S2, S11 and S12 exhibited moderate to low titers (1.11–1.47 log10 cop- ies). Other tested samples were found in moderate range of viral titers (1.47–1.59 log10 copies). The plasmid posi- tive control amplified at a Ct value of 9.67, equivalent to 6.11 log10 copies (~1.27 × 10⁶ copies). No amplification was observed in the healthy (H) and non-template (N) controls (Table 2, Fig. 3B).

Discussion

AMD is a major viral constraint affecting apple production worldwide, and ApNMV has been identified as its predom- inant causal agent in several Asian countries (Noda et al. 2017; Cho et al. 2017; Xing et al. 2018; Shi et al. 2020; Nabi et al. 2020). As apples are propagated vegetatively and ApNMV is graft-transmissible, reliable detection of the virus in planting materials is critical for disease manage- ment and orchard sustainability. Although several molecular techniques such as RT-PCR, multiplex PCR, RT-qPCR and high-throughput sequencing have been applied for ApNMV detection (Nabi et al. 2022, 2023; Khan et al. 2024b), their reliance on purified nucleic acids, expensive instrumenta- tion, and specialized expertise limits the routine use. In this context, isothermal amplification methods such as recombi- nase polymerase amplification (RPA) have gained increas- ing attention due to their simplicity, rapidity, and robustness in plant virus detection (Londoño et al. 2016; Srivastava et al. 2019; Kumar et al. 2021; Zhou et al. 2022; Thapa et al.
2024; Bhardwaj et al. 2025).

The RT-RPA assay developed in the present study offers several advantages over conventional PCR-based approaches. The enhanced performance of RT-RPA can be attributed to its tolerance to plant-derived inhibitors and reduced dependence on high-quality RNA, features that are
particularly advantageous for crude extract-based diagnos-

tics and have been reported for several plant virus systems. Using NaOH:EDTA (1:1) crude sap as template eliminated the requirement for RNA purification, thereby simplifying the workflow and reducing cost and time, consistent with previous studies demonstrating its tolerance to plant inhibi- tors and suitability for crude extract-based virus detection (Baranwal et al. 2007; Mekuria et al. 2014; Tomar et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2023; Diksha et al. 2024). This perfor- mance is consistent with the isothermal amplification char- acteristics reported for RT-RPA-based detection of other plant viruses (Srivastava et al. 2019; Gupta et al. 2024; Kis- han et al. 2024). Importantly, RT-RPA demonstrated higher analytical sensitivity than conventional RT-PCR, particu- larly when crude plant extracts were used as templates. This difference is likely due to the greater tolerance of RT-RPA to inhibitors present in crude plant extracts and its reduced dependence on RNA integrity and reverse transcription efficiency, factors that can limit RT-PCR performance and lead to false-negative results in low-titer samples (Kumar et al. 2025a, b). Similar enhanced sensitivity of RT-RPA over RT-PCR has been reported for chilli veinal mottle virus (Devi et al. 2023), citrus tristeza virus (Sharma et al. 2023) and simultaneous detection of banana streak MY virus and banana bunchy top virus (Bhardwaj et al. 2025).

The assay was highly specific to ApNMV, with no cross- reactivity observed against other common apple viruses such as ASPV, ASGV, ACLSV and ApMV, even under mixed infection conditions, further substantiating its reliability. Field validation across 73 samples revealed higher detec- tion efficiency of RT-RPA (75.3%) compared to RT-PCR (71.2%), in agreement with reports of RPA outperforming PCR under field conditions (Srivastava et al. 2019; Devi et

al. 2023; Kishan et al. 2023). The assay was further simpli- fied through HNB dye-based colorimetric detection, where a distinct shift from violet (negative) to sky blue (positive) provided a clear visual readout concordant with gel electro- phoresis, thus enabling on-site diagnostics without special- ized equipment. Comparable colorimetric detection using HNB has been successfully demonstrated for other pest and pathogens (Priti et al. 2021; Wani et al. 2023; Kumar et al. 2025a, b).

In addition to RT-RPA, we developed a SYBR Green RT-qPCR assay targeting the ApNMV RdRp gene for abso- lute quantification. The assay produced a robust standard curve (R2 = 0.9988) with amplification efficiency of 98.6%, falling within the acceptable range of 90–110% (Li et al. 2009; Kumar et al. 2026), and quantified viral loads rang- ing from ~12.9 to 86.9 copies in field samples. The single- peak melting profiles confirmed amplification specificity. Quantitative assays such as SYBR Green RT-qPCR provide valuable insights into virus epidemiology and facilitate evi- dence-based management decisions. Comparable standard- curve-based absolute quantification approaches have been reported for apple viruses (Winkowska et al. 2016; Kim et al. 2022), grapevine viruses (Fajardo et al. 2017; Morán et al. 2020), and viruses infecting citrus, rice, and tomato (Sharma and Dasgupta 2012; Kokane et al. 2021; Li et al. 2025; Kumar et al. 2026).

Overall, the dual approach combining RT-RPA and RT- qPCR addresses complementary needs in ApNMV manage- ment. RT-RPA provides rapid, sensitive, and field-deployable detection using crude extracts, making it suitable for nurser- ies, quarantine centres, and orchard surveillance. RT-qPCR offers precise quantification of viral load, enabling epidemi- ological studies, evaluation of management strategies, and certification of virus-free planting material. Nevertheless, limitations remain: crude extract-based RT-RPA is slightly less sensitive than RNA-based assays, colorimetric inter- pretation may vary under field conditions, and the cost and supply of RPA reagents may affect scalability. Incorpora- tion of internal amplification controls and multiplexing to simultaneously detect multiple apple viruses would further enhance diagnostic reliability and utility (Jiao et al. 2021).
Conclusion

This study establishes a rapid, sensitive, and field-deploy- able RT-RPA assay for ApNMV using crude sap, eliminat- ing the need for RNA extraction. The assay outperformed RT-PCR in sensitivity, showed high specificity, and was fur- ther simplified with HNB-based colorimetric detection for on-site use. A complementary SYBR Green RT-qPCR assay enabled absolute quantification of viral load, strengthening
Page 11 of 13 34
its utility for epidemiological studies. Together, these assays provide an efficient diagnostic toolkit for routine surveil- lance, certification, and sustainable management of AMD.
